blocks.sub: Injection, poisoning, exfiltration and abuse, engineered as production surfaces

blocks.x: AI Security & Model Protection is delivered by an Achala practice team that stays through industrialization. Achala implements security your auditors can walk alone: control tests that run continuously, findings filed automatically, frameworks mapped to ISO 27001, SOC 2, TISAX and NIS2. Security posture becomes something you show, not something you claim. Who this is for: CISOs and audit committees, and program owners facing TISAX, HIPAA or NIS2 scrutiny.

The scope covers the whole stack: prompt and response paths, retrieval integrity (can an attacker poison the corpus?), model and data exfiltration, agent-tool abuse, and the governance that says which model may touch which data class.
Below: the failure modes specific to model-backed systems, the reference architecture that defends them, and the console that measures the defenses honestly.

Defend the model layer like a production service
blocks.sub: Injection firewalls, corpus integrity and abuse detection, the new surface, engineered

blocks.x: AI security fails when the model is treated as a feature and defended as an afterthought: prompt injection walks through retrieval, corpus poisoning waits weeks to be noticed, and exfiltration rides the tool calls nobody scoped. The defense is layered at the surfaces, an injection firewall before the model (filter chain, not a hopeful system prompt), corpus integrity with signed and versioned documents, a model-data policy that keeps classified data out of prompts by construction, and output guards that redact before tokens reach the user. Abuse detection treats the model endpoint like any other production service: rate signals, intent signals and anomaly detection on the traffic.

Measurement makes it credible: an adversarial red-team eval suite runs in CI (every prompt, guard or model change attacks the defenses), and attack simulations are scored and trended per defense layer. The agent-abuse containment overlay closes the loop for agentic surfaces, tool scoping, spend ceilings and blast-radius limits, because the newest attack surface is the one your own automation provides.

How is AI security different from application security?

The model layer is a new attack surface: prompts are untrusted input, corpora are poisoning targets, agent tools are abuse paths. Classic frameworks never named these, we defend the model layer like a production service, with the same budget discipline.
Can you red-team our models safely?

Yes, red-team drills run against staging twins with rate-limited, logged attacks. Containment and drift-escape rates per technique, injection, jailbreak, poisoning, extraction, become the gate evidence before exposure.
What happens when an adversarial prompt gets through?

Layered defense: the prompt guard classifies, retrieval refuses unverifiable context, and agent tool calls are scoped per session. A technique that escapes one layer hits the next, drift escapes above budget trip the exposure gate.
How do you protect training corpora and RAG indexes?

Corpus integrity is monitored at admission: provenance checks, anomaly detection on document additions, and canary queries that detect poisoning drift. A poisoned corpus fails the gate before it answers a customer.
Who owns model security after handover?
The security engineering team inherits the control plane, the drill calendar, the console with measured rates and the gates, AI security becomes part of the release rhythm, not an annual review.
